How mmsyFM works

Source: vignettes/how-it-works.Rmd
how-it-works.Rmd

This guide describes the model, the calibration of a system and the management analyses. The same text is the Guide tab of the app (run_app()). For a worked example see vignette("mmsyFM").

1. What mmsyFM does

mmsyFM simulates a mixed fishery in which several fleet segments share many stocks, and fishers decide where and whether to fish by expected profit. It is used to

  • find the safeguarded multispecies MSY: the effort limits that give the highest long-term yield (or revenue, or profit) while every stock stays at or above a safeguard such as Bpa = 0.5 Bmsy;
  • compare management schemes: effort caps by segment, closures of metiers (all year or by month), and feedback harvest control rules (HCRs) under assessment error, implementation error, process error and data lags.

It extends the shared-q model of the multispecies MSY app (mmsyapp), in which every stock receives a fixed share of a single effort pool, with a model of fleet behaviour.

The model has four layers: stocks, fleet, behaviour and management. The sections below describe each, then how a system is calibrated (“tuned”), and how the analyses work. The equations are in Appendix A and the search algorithms in Appendix B.

2. Stocks

Each stock is a Schaefer surplus-production pool with intrinsic growth r and carrying capacity K. The year is fished in 12 monthly steps and growth is added once a year on the start-of-year biomass:

B[t+1] = ( B[t] + r B[t] (1 - B[t]/K) - C[t] ) x exp(eta[t])
C[t]   = sum over months of  B[m] (1 - exp(-F[m]))

eta is process error (section 8; zero in deterministic runs). A stock’s monthly F is the sum over metiers of catchability x effective days x the stock’s seasonal availability in that month.

F/Fmsy is measured as a harvest rate. Over a year a stock loses the share h = 1 - exp(-F) of its biomass to fishing. In this discrete model the equilibrium is B/K = 1 - h/r, so hmsy = r/2, and mmsyFM reports F/Fmsy = h / hmsy. With this definition the identity

B/Bmsy + F/Fmsy = 2

holds exactly at equilibrium (the Kobe plot shows every stock on that line). Using r/2 for the instantaneous F would overstate F/Fmsy for fast stocks: for r = 1.4 the instantaneous Fmsy is 1.2, not 0.7 (see ffmsy()).

F cap: persistence at low abundance. A Schaefer stock goes extinct when F/Fmsy >= 2, but heavily fished stocks rarely do: the last fish are scattered, in refuges or not worth the trip. F_cap (column of the species table, in units of Fmsy) limits each stock’s realised F. With F_cap = 1.95 no stock can settle below 2 - 1.95 = 0.05 Bmsy; extra effort on a capped stock catches nothing more, so it becomes “economically extinct” and is left to by-catch. The cap is hard in deterministic runs (equilibrium, tuning) and smooth in stochastic runs, F = (F_nom^-p + F_cap^-p)^(-1/p) with p = 8, so it has no kink. For schooling pelagics (purse seine), whose catch rates hold up as the stock shrinks, a higher cap or none may be more realistic.

Starting depletion. dep_init (B/K, species table) is the biomass at which simulations start; default 1 (unfished). Conditioned systems carry their calibrated depletion, so projections start from the present state.

3. Fleet

  • Metiers are tactic x ground combinations (e.g. trawl on the inner shelf, hook and line on the reef). Each has a daily cost.
  • Catchability Q (metiers x stocks) says how strongly a metier catches each stock; it encodes gear selectivity and the overlap between where a stock lives and where the metier fishes. It can be written directly (e.g. an expert overlap matrix) or derived from a habitat landscape with ms_landscape(): seabed cells (depth, substrate, area), each stock’s depth and substrate preference, each metier’s ground (depth range, substrates) and gear selectivity, giving q = q0 x selectivity x (stock density on the ground / average density). The calibration (section 5) then sets the level of each stock’s column.
  • Segments (e.g. trawl, purse seine, small-scale) have:
    • home metiers and loyalty: the share of their days spent on home metiers; loyalty 1 = zoning (a segment fishes only its own metiers), loyalty < 1 lets part of the days go to any open metier;
    • efficiency: catch per day relative to a specialist (e.g. 0.75 for a mixed vessel, 0.075 for a small-scale vessel-day);
    • a daily cost multiplier;
    • vessel heterogeneity: vessel efficiency varies (lognormal, CV 0.25), so some vessels of a segment break even when others do not;
    • capacity: registered days, the most the segment can fish in a year.

4. Behaviour

Where to fish. Each segment spreads its days over the metiers it can use in proportion to expected profit per day, raised to the power gamma (“how strongly fishers chase profit”):

P(metier m) proportional to  open[m] x max(efficiency x value[m] - cost[m], 0)^gamma

with value[m] the expected revenue per day at current biomass. A segment puts the share loyalty of its days on its home metiers and the rest on all open metiers. gamma = 0 is profit-blind (days spread evenly); with gamma = 1.5, a metier paying twice the profit of another gets 74% of the days.

Whether to fish. Days fished are those of the vessels that break even: each year a segment’s days move (at rate phi, default 0.5) towards capacity x the share of its vessels whose catch covers their costs. When stocks are depleted, trips stop paying and effort falls; when they recover, effort returns. Effort caps (management) can only lower the days further.

5. Calibration: getting the starting point right

A system is calibrated in three steps, normally once per case study:

  1. Daily costs (ms_tune()). At open access the fleet composition is set by costs. ms_tune() solves the daily cost multiplier of each segment so that the open-access equilibrium has the target share of days by segment (e.g. 12 / 6 / 82% for trawl / purse seine / small-scale) and a target status: the weakest stock (e.g. 0.05 Bmsy), the median stock, or the total days.
  2. Stock status (ms_condition()). When the present status of each stock is known (e.g. 2024 depletions from assessments), ms_condition() rescales each stock’s catchability until its equilibrium B/Bmsy matches the target, while ms_tune() keeps the shares of days with the total days fixed (the overall effort level and the catchability scale cannot both be estimated). Targets are limited to a range (default 0.05-1.5 Bmsy); stocks without a target are left free. The step uses F/Fmsy = 2 - target, so it converges in a few iterations; simulations start at the targets, because slow stocks fished near their limit would need centuries to settle from K.
  3. Status quo (ms_status_quo()). The calibrated open-access equilibrium is the reference for everything else: the days by segment it produces are the reference effort that yield curves scale, caps are compared with and HCRs act on.

6. Equilibrium analyses

Yield curves

ms_yield_curve() scales the status-quo days of all segments by a common factor and runs each to equilibrium. The app compares four treatments:

  • Shared q: one effort pool and a fixed catchability per stock, calibrated to reproduce the status-quo F of every stock. Effort raises F on all stocks in the same proportions; there is no behaviour. Solved analytically (ms_shared_q_curve()).
  • Profit-blind: the metier structure and economic exit, but days are spread evenly over each segment’s metiers (gamma = 0).
  • Profit-seeking: days follow expected profit (gamma as set).
  • Profit-seeking + closure: as above with one metier closed all year; its days move to the other metiers (displacement).

All curves pass through the status quo. Shared q gives the classic dome; behaviour flattens it, because effort leaves depleted stocks. The safeguarded yield (all stocks >= Bpa) can be far lower with behaviour: when effort is cut, stocks recover and effort concentrates on the most valuable ground, often the choke stock’s.

Safeguarded MMSY (ms_optimise())

Finds the effort caps that maximise the objective (total yield, revenue, or profit = MEY) at equilibrium, subject to every stock at or above Bpa. The stock at the limit is the choke stock.

  • Levers: one global cap (split across segments in their status-quo proportions) or one cap per segment.
  • Viability floor: with caps per segment, every segment keeps at least this share of the total days, so the optimum cannot shut a segment down.
  • Closures: metiers kept closed during the optimisation.

The search is a zooming grid over the caps, robust to the kinks of a behavioural fleet.

7. Harvest strategies (feedback control)

hcr_effort() builds a rule that sets each segment’s days every year; ms_simulate(..., hcr = rule) runs it in a closed loop.

Each year:

  1. Assessment. Each assessed unit (stock or complex) gets an estimated B/Bmsy = true value x lognormal error (CV assess_cv, optional AR(1)), from data hcr_lag years old (default 2: data of year t-2, assessed in t-1, advice for t).
  2. Responsibility. A segment answers for the stocks it catches as a main fishery: one of the metiers it can use (its home metiers when loyalty > 0) has at least own_q (default 0.5) of the stock’s highest catchability in any metier. With own_q = 0.2 by-catch counts too.
  3. Status of the segment. By default (aggregate = "weighted") it is the mean assessed B/Bmsy of those stocks, weighted by each stock’s potential revenue for the segment (its catchability on the segment’s metiers x price x K): the stocks that make up a fishery drive its effort. The weakest link (aggregate = "min", the most depleted stock decides) is the special, most precautionary case.
  4. Ramp. A segment’s days are a fraction of its full effort, normally the safeguarded-MMSY days from ms_optimise() (or the status-quo days): 1 at or above the trigger Btrig (default 0.5 Bmsy, i.e. at Bpa, as in ICES and GFCM advice; it can differ by segment, e.g. higher for small pelagics), falling linearly to the minimum effort Emin (default 0.1) at Blim (0.25 Bmsy) and below. The rule reduces effort but never closes a segment (Emin = 0 allows a full closure).
  5. Smoothing and implementation. The days may change by at most max_change a year relative to the previous year (0.2 = 20% up or down, as for TAC changes), starting from the current (status-quo) days, so the move to the full effort and later cuts and recoveries are phased; realised days differ from allowed days by implementation error (CV impl_cv).

The weak species are protected in three ways: the full effort itself keeps every stock at or above Bpa at equilibrium (the safeguard of the MMSY optimisation); the ramp cuts a segment when the stocks it fishes decline; and a choke stock can be protected by a closure of the metiers that drive it (below) instead of cutting whole fleets.

Mixed fleets. A mixed or generalist segment fishes many metiers, so it answers for many stocks. Under the weakest link it is cut whenever any of them is low, together with the specialist that targets it: one weak stock constrains every fleet that touches it, and with many depleted, slow stocks and noisy assessments the fleets stay at the minimum effort for decades. The value-weighted status avoids this while the full effort and closures keep the safeguard.

Alternatives to cutting days (arguments of hcr_effort()):

  • close: protect a choke stock by closing the metiers that drive it (catchability >= close_q, default 0.5, of its highest) for a share of the time that ramps from 0 at Btrig_close to fully closed at Blim; that stock is then left out of the effort rule.
  • assessed: only some stocks are assessed (e.g. 4 of 20); the rule ignores the rest, which may then decline unnoticed.
  • assign: nominal assignment of each stock to one segment for management (e.g. Dentex to the demersal fleet), as is common in practice; other segments still catch it but are not cut for it.
  • complexes: stocks assessed as a pooled group (e.g. “reef fish”), from pooled biomass or a pooled catch rate. Pooling can hide a weak member.

Metier closures. Management can also close one or more metiers outright, all year or for some months, and for all or part of their ground (an area closure), independently of stock status: ms_closure(sys, c("TR_inner", "TR_mid"), months = 2:5) gives the open share by month and metier, passed as open to ms_simulate(). Displaced days move to the open metiers by expected profit. In practice this is often more realistic than a closure triggered by one species’ assessment. The app compares “metier closures only” (otherwise uncontrolled fleet) and “HCR + metier closures” with the other rules.

Tuning triggers (ms_tune_hcr()). Runs a grid of effort (and closure) triggers with common random numbers (every trigger sees the same random errors) and picks the trigger with the highest yield whose risk meets the limit, by default: the worst stock below Bpa at most 5% of the time.

8. Uncertainty

  • Process error on the surplus-production equation (JABBA form), with AR(1) autocorrelation and optional correlation between stocks:
    • its SD scales with r: sd = 0.05 (r / 0.057)^0.68, i.e. about 0.05 for sharks (r = 0.057) and 0.4 for anchovy (r = 1.2) (proc_sd_from_r());
    • it increases at low biomass, following JABBA’s proc.dyn function (relsig_jabba()): about 1.5x at 0.5 Bmsy and 4x at 0.05 Bmsy, so depleted stocks are more volatile;
    • centring: "median" (as JABBA’s lognormal) has no drift; "mean" is mean-unbiased, so the median drifts down when the SD is large (stochastic depensation).
  • Assessment error and data lag (section 7).
  • Implementation error on the allowed days by segment.
  • Effort noise: year-to-year variation of effort and catch rates by segment, in every run, regulated or not.

9. Performance statistics

ms_perf() computes performance statistics of a set of runs (one per rule or management procedure) over the evaluation years (default the last 20), per iteration, and returns them as a long data.table in the format of the FLR package mseviz (mp, biol, statistic, name, desc, year, iter, data), so they can also be passed to mseviz::plotBPs(), mseviz::plotTOs() or mseviz::perfTable().

  • By stock (biol = stock code): median B/Bmsy and F/Fmsy, catch/MSY, P(B < Blim), P(B < Bpa), P(B > 0.8 Bmsy) and P(Kobe green).
  • By segment: mean days fished.
  • System (biol = "All"): total catch, revenue, profit, days, catch relative to the sum of single-stock MSYs, the average annual variation of catch and of days, the mean number of stocks below Bpa, P(any stock below Blim) and the lowest B/Bmsy reached.

Probabilities are the share of years (per iteration) and are summarised by their mean over iterations. Presentation:

  • plot_bps(): boxplots by rule (10th-90th percentiles), probabilities as points, with target and limit lines (the style of mseviz::plotBPs()); for the system or for selected stocks (one row of panels per stock);
  • plot_tradeoffs(): medians and 10th-90th percentile ranges of each statistic against catch (or revenue, profit, days);
  • plot_quilt(): colour-coded decision tables, either rules x statistics (green = best, red = worst within each statistic, by its preferred direction) or stocks x rules for one statistic, with optional absolute classes for probabilities (green at or below a risk limit, amber up to twice the limit, red above);
  • ms_perf_table(): medians with 10th-90th percentiles as a table.

The earlier summary ms_performance() (one row per rule) is kept.

Appendix A. Model equations

Notation: stocks \(s\), metiers \(j\), segments \(g\), years \(t\), months \(m\).

A1. Stock dynamics (discrete Schaefer with monthly fishing)

Within a year, each month removes catch from the biomass (Baranov, no growth within the year):

\[F_{s,m} = a_{s,m} \sum_j q_{js} \tilde E_{j,m}, \qquad C_{s,m} = B_{s,m} \left(1 - e^{-F_{s,m}}\right), \qquad B_{s,m+1} = B_{s,m} - C_{s,m}\]

with \(a_{s,m}\) the seasonal availability of stock \(s\), \(q_{js}\) the catchability of metier \(j\) and \(\tilde E_{j,m}\) the effective days (days x efficiency x open share). Growth is added once a year on the start-of-year biomass, with process error \(\eta\):

\[B_{s,t+1} = \max\left( B_{s,t} + r_s B_{s,t} \left(1 - \frac{B_{s,t}}{K_s}\right) - C_{s,t}, \quad 0.005 K_s \right) e^{\eta_{s,t}}, \qquad C_{s,t} = \sum_m C_{s,m}\]

The floor at 0.005 K (as in JABBA) matters for fast stocks: with r > 1, a large positive shock can take a stock above K, and the logistic update from there can turn negative (overshoot); without the floor the stock would be absorbed at zero.

A2. Reference points and F/Fmsy

A year of fishing removes the share \(h_{s,t} = 1 - e^{-F_{s,t}}\) with \(F_{s,t} = \sum_m F_{s,m}\). The deterministic equilibrium is

\[\frac{B_s}{K_s} = 1 - \frac{h_s}{r_s}, \qquad h_{MSY} = \frac{r_s}{2}, \qquad B_{MSY} = \frac{K_s}{2}, \qquad MSY = \frac{r_s K_s}{4}\]

so that, with \(F/F_{MSY} \equiv h / h_{MSY}\),

\[\frac{B}{B_{MSY}} + \frac{F}{F_{MSY}} = 2 .\]

A3. F cap

With cap \(\phi_s\) (units of \(F_{MSY}\)), the largest annual harvest rate is \(h^{max}_s = \min(\phi_s r_s / 2, 1)\), i.e. \(F^{max}_s = -\ln(1 - h^{max}_s)\), applied monthly as \(F^{max}_s / 12\). The equilibrium floor is \(B/B_{MSY} \ge 2 - \phi_s\). The realised monthly F is

\[F = \min\left(F^{nom}, F^{max}\right) \quad \text{(hard)}, \qquad F = \left( (F^{nom})^{-p} + (F^{max})^{-p} \right)^{-1/p} \quad \text{(smooth, } p = 8\text{)} .\]

A4. Process error

\[\eta_{s,t} = \rho \eta_{s,t-1} + \sqrt{1 - \rho^2} \varepsilon_{s,t}, \qquad \varepsilon_{s,t} \sim N\left(0, \sigma_{s,t}^2\right)\]

centred on the median (as above) or on the mean (\(\eta - \sigma^2/2\)). The SD depends on r and on depletion (JABBA proc.dyn):

\[\sigma_{s,t} = \sigma_s^0 \frac{g(B_{s,t}/B_{MSY,s})}{g(1)}, \qquad \sigma_s^0 = 0.05 \left(\frac{r_s}{0.057}\right)^{0.68}, \qquad g(x) = a + \frac{1 - a}{1 + (x/c)^d}\]

with \(a = 0.128\), \(c = 0.223\), \(d = 1.326\), capped at 1. Correlation between stocks mixes a common draw: \(\varepsilon_s = \sqrt{1-\omega} z_s + \sqrt{\omega} z_0\).

A5. Effort allocation: the profit preference

The expected revenue per effective day of metier \(j\) in month \(m\), at current biomass, is

\[V_{j,m} = \sum_s p_s q_{js} a_{s,m} B_{s,m}\]

with price \(p_s\). A vessel of segment \(g\) (efficiency \(e_{gj}\), times the mean efficiency \(\bar v_g\) of its active vessels) expects the profit per day \(e_{gj} \bar v_g V_{j,m} - \kappa_g c_j\), with \(c_j\) the daily cost of the metier and \(\kappa_g\) the segment’s cost multiplier. Its utility is

\[u_{gj} = o_{j} \max\left(e_{gj} \bar v_g V_{j,m} - \kappa_g c_j , 0\right)^{\gamma}\]

(\(o_j\) the open share, \(\gamma\) the strength of the preference; \(\gamma = 0\) gives \(u = 1\) for every open metier). With home metiers \(H_g\) and loyalty \(\lambda_g\), the segment’s days \(E_{g,m}\) are allocated as

\[E_{gj,m} = E_{g,m} \left( \lambda_g \frac{u_{gj} 1[j \in H_g]}{\sum_{k \in H_g} u_{gk}} + (1 - \lambda_g) \frac{u_{gj}}{\sum_k u_{gk}} \right), \qquad \tilde E_{j,m} = o_j \sum_g e_{gj} \bar v_g E_{gj,m}\]

A segment’s days are spread over the months by a fixed seasonal pattern.

A6. Entry and exit (vessel heterogeneity)

Vessel efficiency is lognormal with mean 1: \(v \sim LN(\mu, \sigma_v^2)\), \(\sigma_v^2 = \ln(1 + CV^2)\), \(\mu = -\sigma_v^2 / 2\). From last year’s revenue \(R_g\) and cost \(D_g\) per day of a vessel of mean efficiency (weighted by its allocation), a vessel breaks even when \(v \ge v^* = D_g / R_g\). The share of vessels that break even, and the mean efficiency of the active ones, are

\[P_g = 1 - \Phi\left(\frac{\ln v^* - \mu}{\sigma_v}\right), \qquad \bar v_g = \frac{1}{P_g} \Phi\left(\frac{\mu + \sigma_v^2 - \ln v^*}{\sigma_v}\right)\]

and the segment’s days move towards the days of those vessels, within the cap \(\bar E_g\) (management) and the capacity \(\mathcal{K}_g\):

\[E_{g,t+1} = E_{g,t} + \varphi \left( \min\left(\bar E_g, \mathcal{K}_g P_g\right) - E_{g,t} \right), \qquad \varphi = 0.5 .\]

A7. Economics

Revenue and cost of a year, and profit:

\[R_t = \sum_s p_s C_{s,t}, \qquad D_t = \sum_g \kappa_g \sum_j c_j E_{gj,t}, \qquad \Pi_t = R_t - D_t .\]

Without a cost column, the daily cost of a metier is a share (0.4) of its unfished revenue rate, \(c_j = 0.4 \sum_s p_s q_{js} K_s \bar a_s\).

A8. Harvest control rule (effort)

The assessed status is \(\hat b_{u,t} = b_{u,t-L} e^{\epsilon_{u,t}}\) with \(b = B/B_{MSY}\) of unit \(u\) (stock or complex), lag \(L\) and lognormal error \(\epsilon\) (CV assess_cv, optional AR(1)). Segment \(g\) answers for the units \(U_g\) it catches as a main fishery (\(\max_{j \in H_g} q_{js} \ge \theta \max_j q_{js}\), \(\theta\) = own_q). Its status is the value-weighted mean (or, for the weakest link, the minimum)

\[\hat b_{g,t} = \sum_{u \in U_g} w_{gu} \hat b_{u,t}, \qquad w_{gu} \propto \sum_{s \in u} p_s K_s \sum_{j \in H_g} q_{js} \qquad \left(\text{or } \hat b_{g,t} = \min_{u \in U_g} \hat b_{u,t}\right)\]

and its fraction of the reference (full) days \(E^{ref}_g\), the safeguarded-MMSY days or the status-quo days, is

\[f_{g,t} = E_{min} + (1 - E_{min}) \min\left(1, \max\left(0, \frac{\hat b_{g,t} - B_{lim}}{B_{trig,g} - B_{lim}}\right)\right)\]

limited to \((1 - \Delta) f_{g,t-1} \le f_{g,t} \le (1 + \Delta) \max(f_{g,t-1}, 0.05)\) (with \(f_{g,0} = E_{g,0} / E^{ref}_g\), the current days relative to the reference). The cap is \(\bar E_{g,t} = f_{g,t} E^{ref}_g e^{\xi_{g,t}}\) with implementation error \(\xi\). A closure for unit \(u\) sets the open share of the metiers that drive it (\(q_{js} \ge\) close_q \(\max_j q_{js}\)) to the same ramp, from 0 at \(B_{lim}\) to 1 at its own trigger.

A9. Calibration

ms_tune() solves the log cost multipliers \(\log \kappa_g\) so that the open-access equilibrium meets \(G\) conditions: the day shares of the first \(G - 1\) segments and one status target. ms_condition() updates each targeted stock’s catchability column by

\[q_{js} \leftarrow q_{js} \left(\frac{2 - b^*_s}{F_s / F_{MSY,s}}\right)^{0.8}\]

with target \(b^*_s\) (from \(B/B_{MSY} + F/F_{MSY} = 2\)), keeping each metier’s cost proportional to its unfished revenue, and re-runs ms_tune() with the total days fixed.

Appendix B. Algorithms

  • Equilibria are found by simulation: a run of 200-500 years, averaged over its last 10-30 years. Many scenarios (rows) run in one vectorised call.
  • ms_optimise(): a zooming grid search over the caps in \(\log(1 + E)\). Each round runs \(n^d\) candidates (\(d\) levers) to equilibrium in one call, keeps the best feasible one (every stock at or above Bpa) and shrinks the box around it (5 rounds). No bisection or gradient method is used: with fleet behaviour the safeguard is not monotone in effort (cutting effort can concentrate it on the most valuable ground and lower the weakest stock), and the objective has flat stretches and small kinks from vessel exit.
  • ms_tune(): Newton’s method on \(\log \kappa_g\) with a numerical Jacobian (\(G + 1\) perturbed systems in one call), bounded steps, and the best iterate kept.
  • ms_condition(): the fixed-point update of A9, alternated with ms_tune(); simulations start at the targets so slow stocks need not settle from K.
  • ms_tune_hcr(): a grid of triggers run with common random numbers (every trigger sees the same process, assessment and implementation errors); the highest yield that meets the risk limit is chosen.
